description: Some guys intrested in Mars and decided to make a map on it. Gaining skills and knowledge along the way
summary:
We developed an interactive user interface to support future astronauts in safely planning and carrying out extravehicular activities (EVAs), or spacewalks, on Mars. It addresses the challenges of navigating unfamiliar Martian terrain through a topographical map and a 3D layered map, helping users visualise elevation, slopes and geographical features.

The interface brings together environmental and terrain information to support astronaut safety and mission planning. This includes surface hazards, radiation levels, atmospheric conditions, terrain gradients and possible chemical compositions of Martian soil. By presenting this information in one place, the project aims to help astronauts make informed decisions, plan suitable routes and identify scientifically valuable locations.

The project uses NASA resources, including the Perseverance Rover Record Drive Path Animation and NASA/JPL’s Mars Trek for rover-path visualisation and 3D planetary mapping.

Its significance lies in astronaut safety, route planning and scientific exploration. It could help crews navigate challenging terrain, avoid hazards and reach geological locations such as Cheyava Falls. It could also help scientists identify areas for further investigation and sampling. Beyond Mars, similar mapping methods could support disaster response, remote navigation and the assessment of hazardous environments on Earth.
details:
Our project is an interactive Martian mapping interface designed to support future astronauts in planning and carrying out extravehicular activities (EVAs), or spacewalks, on Mars. It provides a topographical map and a 3D layered map that allow users to explore Martian terrain, understand elevation differences and identify geographical features that may affect their routes.

The interface also presents demonstrations of additional safety features, including potential surface hazards, radiation levels, atmospheric conditions, terrain gradients and possible chemical compositions of Martian soil. These represent planned capabilities that could be developed further using reliable scientific datasets.

We used publicly available NASA resources, including NASA's Perseverance Rover Record Drive Path Animation and NASA/JPL's Mars Trek for rover-path visualisation and 3D planetary mapping.

The main benefits include improving terrain awareness, supporting route planning and demonstrating how environmental information could contribute to astronaut safety. It could also help scientists identify geological locations, such as Cheyava Falls, for further investigation.

Our creativity lies in combining topographical mapping, 3D visualisation and proposed environmental safety features into one interactive interface.

We developed the project using HTML, TSX, CSS, TypeScript, JSON and YAML files, with Visual Studio Code and GitHub as development tools. We used a laptop for programming and mobile phones for testing. Additional project resources included PDF, JPG and PPTX files. Our team tested the interface on mobile phones and compared its map presentation with our expected design.

Ultimately, our intended impact is to demonstrate how interactive mapping and NASA planetary resources could contribute to safer, more informed and effective future human exploration of Mars.
